<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 9 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Newton-Cartan Theory</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">9.2</span> Newton’s Axioms</h1></header>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>To decide which curves can describe particles and which vectors can describe forces, tangent vectors are classified according to their time content. A tangent vector <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p \in T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> is called</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><strong>future directed</strong> if <span class="math inline">\((dt)_p(\mathcal{X}_p) &gt; 0\)</span>,</p></li>
<li><p><strong>spatial</strong> if <span class="math inline">\((dt)_p(\mathcal{X}_p) = 0\)</span>, i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p \in T_p\mathcal{S}_{t(p)}\)</span>,</p></li>
<li><p><strong>past directed</strong> if <span class="math inline">\((dt)_p(\mathcal{X}_p) &lt; 0\)</span>.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>A vector field <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_\gamma\)</span> along a curve <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span> is spatial if all its values <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_\gamma(\lambda)\)</span> are.</p></li>
<li><p>The <strong>worldline</strong> of a particle of mass <span class="math inline">\(m &gt; 0\)</span> is a smooth curve <span class="math inline">\(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\)</span> with future-directed velocity, <span class="math inline">\((dt)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) = (t \circ \gamma)'(\lambda) &gt; 0\)</span> <span class="math inline">\(\forall \lambda \in \mathbb{R}\)</span>: particles always move forward in absolute time, crossing each absolute space at most once. A <strong>force</strong> is a spatial vector field <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{F}_\gamma\)</span>.</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><strong>Newton I:</strong> if no force acts on the particle, its worldline is an autoparallel, <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{v_\gamma} v_\gamma = 0\)</span>. This is not merely the case <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{F}_\gamma = 0\)</span> of Newton II, but a measurement prescription: free particles determine <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span>, i.e. what “straight” means. Gravity is not regarded as a force, but encoded in <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span><sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-3" id="fnref-3" aria-label="Footnote 3">3</a></sup>.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Newton II:</strong> if a force <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{F}_\gamma\)</span> acts on the particle, its worldline satisfies <span class="math inline">\(a_\gamma = \mathcal{F}_\gamma / m\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(a_\gamma = \nabla_{v_\gamma} v_\gamma\)</span> its acceleration. Forces are thus measured as deviations from the autoparallels defined by Newton I.</p></li>
</ol></li>
<li><p><strong>Newton II selects absolute time as parameter.</strong> Forces are spatial, so Newton II, <span class="math inline">\(a_\gamma = \mathcal{F}_\gamma / m\)</span>, requires the acceleration of every worldline to be spatial, <span class="math inline">\((dt)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( a_\gamma(\lambda) \big) = 0\)</span>. Whether it is spatial, however, depends on how the worldline is parametrized: traversing the same path with a different parametrization changes <span class="math inline">\(a_\gamma\)</span>, and in general gives it a time component. The goal is to find the parametrizations for which <span class="math inline">\(a_\gamma\)</span> is spatial, i.e. those in which Newton II can hold. Write <span class="math inline">\(\tau \coloneqq t \circ \gamma\)</span> for the absolute time along the worldline as a function of its parameter, and, in a chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\((dt)_{\gamma(\lambda)} = \mathtt{t}_k^{\gamma(\lambda)} \, (dx^k)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\)</span>.</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>Time content of the velocity.</em> By definition of the differential, the time content of the velocity is the rate at which absolute time advances along the worldline,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
                    \tau'(\lambda) = (dt)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big)
                    = \mathtt{t}_k^{\gamma(\lambda)} \, \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) &gt; 0,
                \end{align*}</span>  positive since worldlines are future directed.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Time content of the acceleration.</em> Differentiating once more, and using uniform flow,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
                    \tau''(\lambda)
                    &amp;= \underbrace{\frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ \mathtt{t}_k^{\gamma(\lambda)} \Big]}_{\substack{= \, v_{\gamma(\lambda)}(\mathtt{t}_k) \\ = \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \partial x_i\left\lfloor \mathtt{t}_k \right\rceil(\gamma(\lambda))}}
                    \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)
                    + \mathtt{t}_k^{\gamma(\lambda)} \, \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \\
                    &amp;= \Gamma^j_{ki}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \mathtt{t}_j^{\gamma(\lambda)} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)
                    + \mathtt{t}_j^{\gamma(\lambda)} \, \ddot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \\
                    &amp;= \mathtt{t}_j^{\gamma(\lambda)} \underbrace{\Big( \ddot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(\lambda)
                    + \Gamma^j_{ki}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \dot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \Big)}_{\text{components of } a_\gamma(\lambda) \text{ by } (\ast\ast)}
                    = (dt)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( a_\gamma(\lambda) \big),
                \end{align*}</span>  where in the second line uniform flow was used in components (Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>),  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
                    0 = \Big( \nabla_{v_{\gamma(\lambda)}} dt \Big)_k
                    = \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, \partial x_i\left\lfloor \mathtt{t}_k \right\rceil\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big)
                    - \Gamma^j_{ki}\big( \gamma(\lambda) \big) \, \mathtt{t}_j^{\gamma(\lambda)} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda),
                \end{align*}</span>  and the summed index <span class="math inline">\(k \to j\)</span> was relabelled in the last term. The acceleration thus has a time component precisely when absolute time does not grow linearly with the parameter.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Spatial acceleration.</em> Hence <span class="math inline">\(a_\gamma\)</span> is spatial if and only if  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
                    \tau'' = 0
                    \longleftrightarrow
                    \tau(\lambda) = c_1 \lambda + c_2, \qquad c_1 = \tau' &gt; 0,
                \end{align*}</span>  i.e. if and only if the parameter is absolute time, up to the choice of units (<span class="math inline">\(c_1\)</span>) and origin (<span class="math inline">\(c_2\)</span>). In any other parametrization, <span class="math inline">\(a_\gamma\)</span> has a time component which no spatial force can match, and Newton II cannot hold. Choosing <span class="math inline">\(c_1 = 1\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(c_2 = 0\)</span>, every worldline is <strong>parametrized by absolute time</strong>, <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \equiv t\)</span>, and the temporal component of Newton II then holds identically.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>Uniform flow is essential: without it, step 2 would contain the extra term <span class="math inline">\(\big( \nabla_{v_{\gamma(\lambda)}} dt \big)\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big)\)</span>, and spatial accelerations would no longer correspond to parametrizations by absolute time.</p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-footnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-3"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-3" aria-label="Back to the text">3</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Why this is possible on spacetime, but not on space, is discussed in Appendix <span class="dg-xref dg-xref-pending" data-label="section_Laplace_Question">B.21.4</span>.</p></div></div></div>
